blocks.text: Bonobos have long had a reputation as the hippies of the ape world. Famously nonaggressive, their matriarchal societies, strong female friendships and largely vegetarian diets have stood in stark contrast to the macho bloodlust of their two closest relatives — chimpanzees and humans.
New research published in Current Biology upends a deep-seated understanding about bonobos and, as a result, could change our understanding of how early humans lived, worked and ate.
Female bonobos, it turns out, aren’t just fruit-eating pacifists, but vicious hunters.

Bonobos are as closely related to humans as chimps. New evidence that female apes are the primary hunters in their troops could radically alter the prevailing model of early human societies, in which men felled big game like bison and antelope, while women engaged in less risky tasks like gathering berries and nuts.

“It really does challenge this idea of the male warrior — that the male hunter is the ancestral model that we should be leaning on,” said Jake Brooker, a primatologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work.

Notions of an ancestral “man the hunter” have long been kicked about by anthropologists and ethnographers. The idea was largely based on studies of living hunter-gatherer societies, like the San people of southern Africa, in which men dominate hunting and fighting.

“If people go out and study a tribe in the Bornean jungle, if they go to Bushmen,” said Gottfried Hohmann, a primatologist at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior and lead author of the study, “it is usually men that are more active in hunting.”
